events.ai_basis: The proof is due to GPT 6 Astra (quoted by whataifound.org from the OpenAI PDF). Also, from Weijie Su's post: 'Announcing that GPT-6 Astra has pushed the prime gap to 186, with Lean formalization!'

why: The statement asks only whether there are infinitely many twin primes, which is equivalent to liminf(p_{n+1}-p_n) = 2. I read the bounded-gap constant H1 as the quantity whose value the conjecture fixes, so the improvements to H1 (Zhang, Maynard, Polymath8b, Stadlmann 240, Kintali and Song-Yue 236, Axiom 212, OpenAI 186) are answered `bound` rather than `variant`. Chen's 'prime or semiprime' theorem changes the question itself, so it is `variant`. The long-gaps paper is about a different quantity (maximal gaps), so it is also `variant`. The Axiom 246 Lean release formalises known results, which makes it `none`. Every amateur claim of a full proof has the F10 signals together: a landmark claim, no uptake, the field still calling the problem open, and self-publishing or marginal venues. Those are `not_credible`. Taha's is `knocked_down` because of a specific gap in the induction that nobody has answered. On AI: OpenAI 186 is `generated`, on the paper's own (secondhand) attribution of the proof to GPT-6 Astra. Kintali and Axiom 212 list no systems credited with mathematics, so both are `none`; AxiomProver produced only the Lean certificate.
doubts: Close call: someone could argue that bounds on H1 are a variant question and not a bound on the twin prime statement. I chose `bound` because the conjecture is exactly H1 = 2. The GPT-6 Astra attribution is quoted from secondary sources because the PDF was unreadable. Kintali's 'I proved H1 <= 236 using AI' was not placed in ai.systems, so I answered `none`; if that is treated as a credit, it would be at most `assisted` with no model named. The Lean development behind the 186 result is conditional on three axioms, and its numerics are certified only by Python.
